reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes BitClub participation by asking viewers to pay a $99 partnership fee and purchase cryptocurrency-mining pools costing $500 to $3,500, while claiming recurring wallet proceeds and daily withdrawals. It also presents Clubcoin bonuses, forecast appreciation, account interest, and compensation from recruited partners and binary teams, then invites viewers to make contact through Skype. The material does not establish whether mining, payouts, withdrawals, token value, or participant losses actually occurred.

opening.argument: The presentation distinguishes a forecast from an established outcome: Clubcoin is described as being forecast to rise, and viewers are told they can leave it in their account or exchange it. That is a promotional account of a speculative offer, not proof that appreciation or mining proceeds are guaranteed. The material itself does not establish that the forecast came true, that withdrawals occurred, or that participants earned money; a judge should not infer deception merely from claims whose results are unverified.

the withdrawal from which is easy every day

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening identifies prices and described payouts, but those details do not establish that the claims were false or that viewers were guaranteed a return. Its own account acknowledges that whether mining, payouts, withdrawals, or token value occurred is unestablished. The forecast is expressly framed as a forecast, not a certainty; uncertainty about performance is not evidence of deception.

citations.quote: is forecast to grow to $ 10-15 per coin

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling one Clubcoin price statement a forecast does not qualify the broader presentation's promised-sounding daily proceeds and partner compensation. The speaker describes daily percentages, wallet credit, and withdrawals as features of the pools, then outlines income from invited partners and teams. Unverified outcomes do not erase the solicitation's concrete claims about how participants can earn.

opening.argument: This is structured as an explanatory walkthrough of a marketing plan: it introduces cryptocurrency mining, compares pool packages, then breaks down how the stated bonuses and point cycles are calculated. The speaker even describes it as a short presentation and offers to answer questions. Those features support reading the video as an explanation of a business model, not as a demonstration that the model succeeded or as proof that every described mechanism is fraudulent.

citations.quote: This was a short presentation under the BITCLUBnetwork company.
The next bonus, which we will analyze, is a cyclical bonus for building 2 teams.
If you have any questions, feel free to contact me over Skype.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats the presentation's explanation of compensation as proof of a scam, but describing a partner program is not itself proof that it operated deceptively. The presentation supplies figures and a worked cycle; the record does not establish whether anyone joined, received payment, or lost money. Contact information for questions is consistent with a presenter inviting follow-up, not evidence of a concealed mechanism.

citations.quote: If you have any questions, feel free to contact me over Skype.
by this principle a binary is calculated in its full depth

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial-like format does not change what is being taught: the presentation explains recurring rewards tied to invited partners and team structures, alongside paid pool packages. Its detailed calculations make the recruitment-linked compensation central rather than incidental. A presentation can be educational in style while still promoting a suspect scheme.

citations.quote: The bonus is distributed in the following way From the 1st and 2nd personally invited partner we get every time from their automatic reinvest by 10%
The next bonus, which we will analyze, is a cyclical bonus for building 2 teams.

opening.argument: The offer is presented as a paid service arrangement: buyers pay for pool packages, which the speaker says rent company equipment for cryptocurrency mining over a stated period. The video also lays out package prices and what each package includes. The record does not establish whether the company actually mined, whether payouts were made, or whether any viewer was recruited; the presence of prices and referral terms alone does not resolve those questions or establish a scam mechanism.

citations.quote: When buying a pool, you essentially rent out equipment from the company to acquire cryptocurrency for six hundred days.
POOL under number one with a price of $ 500 pool under number two worth $ 1,000 pool under number 3 with a price of $ 2,000
If you have any questions, feel free to contact me over Skype.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The listed prices and mining-equipment description are compatible with a paid service; they do not prove that the service was fictional. The opening also concedes that mining and payouts are not established. Although the presentation describes partner bonuses, the record does not show that participants were recruited or paid, and it does not establish that referrals were the only source of value.

citations.quote: you essentially rent out equipment from the company to acquire cryptocurrency for six hundred days.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The service framing cannot account for the presentation's extensive compensation plan: it describes bonuses from personally invited partners, their recruits, and binary team cycles. Pool purchases are not merely ordinary retail prices when the same presentation ties them to recurring returns and recruitment-based rewards. The absence of proof of actual payouts does not neutralize the promotional mechanism shown.
